figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Any3R is a feed-forward model that reconstructs a scene and its camera poses from views of any mix of central cameras.
figures.headline: Any3R reconstructs one scene and its camera poses from a mix of pinhole, fisheye and panoramic views.
citing_sentences: Mixing cameras of different types in one reconstruction, such as a pinhole view, a fisheye frame and a panorama of one scene as in Fig. 1, is harder still.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Motivation. Read from the pixel grid (ii), a patch position stands for a different direction and a pixel for a different solid angle on every lens (i), and the ray field (iii) corrects both. In the bottom row the ray field is withheld, so the backbone reads every frame as a panorama and the reconstruction follows that reading, which is correct only at $360^{\circ}$.
figures.headline: Without the ray field, the backbone reads every frame as a panorama, so the reconstruction is correct only for a 360° lens.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview. The ray field $\bm{R}$ of each view gives its patches angular coordinates for the rotary encoding in intra-frame attention, and the heads predict the camera poses and a radial distance $d$ per pixel, decoded as $\bm{X}=d\bm{R}$. In training, the point loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pt}}$ compares $\bm{X}$ with the ground truth $\bm{X}^{\mathrm{gt}}$, and the solid angle $\mathrm{d}\Omega$ of the same $\bm{R}$ weighs the error of each pixel, shown here on the panorama, where cells of equal pixel count cover unequal areas of the sphere.
figures.headline: Each view's ray field sets the rotary coordinates of its patches and weights each pixel's point-loss error by its solid angle.
citing_sentences: Two of its parts rely on the pixel grid, the rotary positional encoding and the per-pixel training loss, and Any3R gives $\bm{R}$ to both, as Fig. 3 shows.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison with the camera-aware methods. One camera per row, every method fused with its own predicted poses and rendered from one viewpoint per row. Cells marked n/a are structural, since Argus accepts only full panoramas and Wid3R’s camera classes cannot represent the $200^{\circ}$ KB4 lens. MapA-ray is MapAnything given the true ray field, and PaGeR, which predicts no pose, is not shown.
figures.headline: On every camera shown, Any3R returns the whole room, while other camera-aware methods bend or fold it on some lenses.
citing_sentences: In the typical scenes of Fig. 4, whose Acc for Any3R lies between the quartiles of its cell, PanoVGGT bends a pinhole frame into a bowl and MapA-ray still folds the equirectangular room despite the true ray field, while Any3R returns the room on every lens.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Zero-shot reconstruction on real fisheye lenses. Per dataset, the two samples from different scenes on which Any3R leads the zero-shot methods shown most (Wid3R† is trained on ScanNet++). Poses and alignment as in Tab. 2; the highest $30\%$ of each cloud is removed so the room is seen from above.
figures.headline: On real fisheye rooms, Any3R stays close to ground truth where other zero-shot methods bend the scene into curved shells.
citing_sentences: In Fig. 5, the other zero-shot methods bend the FIORD rooms into curved shells, while Any3R stays close to the ground truth.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Eight central camera models, seven methods, one scene per row. Every method fuses the same three native views with its own predicted poses and is placed in the ground-truth frame by one similarity transform, and the highest $30\%$ of each indoor cloud is removed so the room is seen from above. Column MapAny. is MapAnything and Any3R∗ is Any3R without its ray map.
figures.headline: From 180° on, other methods often flatten or fold the room across the eight central cameras, sometimes losing relative pose.
citing_sentences: In the typical scenes of Fig. 6, from $180^{\circ}$ on they place the parts of a frame that look sideways or backwards in front of the camera, flattening the room or folding it into a shell, and VGGT and DA3 often lose the relative pose as well.

Any3R∗, our model without its ray map, assumes an equirectangular grid and reads every frame as a panorama, and its error rises sharply on every lens but the equirectangular one, where that assumption holds and the two rows coincide, so the gain comes from the ray map; in Fig. 6 it bends a pinhole frame into a bowl.

Fig. 6 in the main text draws a different scene in each row, which shows the range of content the benchmark covers but means that rows cannot be compared with one another: a difference between two rows mixes a change of camera with a change of scene.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: One Matterport3D scene, all eight central camera models, all seven methods. Identical protocol to Fig. 6. The scene is fixed, so the vertical axis is field of view alone.
figures.headline: On one fixed Matterport3D scene, changing only the camera across eight models isolates the effect of field of view on each method.
citing_sentences: Fig. 7 holds the scene fixed and varies only the camera, so the vertical axis isolates field of view.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Projection of the thirteen camera models of Tab. 16. Left of each pair, a section through the camera centre $O$ shows probe rays spaced $15^{\circ}$ apart in incidence angle $\theta$, and $30^{\circ}$ apart for ERP, one colour per angle. Each travels from the scene to $O$ (solid) and on to its image point (dashed) on the image plane, a focal length $f$ behind $O$, so the spacing of the dots is the model’s $r(\theta)$. ERP and ERP-Crop are seen from above, their image being the sphere of radius $f$ unrolled, and Cylindrical from the side, its image the cylinder wall a distance $f$ in front. Right of each pair, the same probes in 3D, from their image points through $O$ to the unit sphere, with the image’s rows and columns drawn on the sphere in grey. Here $\phi$ and $\lambda$ are azimuth and elevation, $u$ and $v$ image coordinates, $\rho=\tan\theta$ and $d=\sqrt{\sin^{2}\theta+(\xi+\cos\theta)^{2}}$. Every camera is built as in the benchmark, with the declared field of view reaching half the image height, $k_{1}=-0.18$ and $k_{2}=0.02$ for Brown–Conrady together with the tangential terms $p_{1}=8\times 10^{-4}$ and $p_{2}=-6\times 10^{-4}$, $\omega=0.9$ for FOV/ATAN, $\xi=1.6$ for MEI, $(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})=(0.04,-0.01,0.002,-0.0003)$ for KB4, $\xi=0.25$ and $\alpha=0.55$ for Double-Sphere, $\alpha=0.55$ and $\beta=1$ for EUCM, and a vertical field of view of $90^{\circ}$ for ERP-Crop and Cylindrical.
figures.headline: Thirteen camera models are drawn as cross-sections and ray fields, showing how each lens spaces its rays.
citing_sentences: Fig. 8 draws how each of the thirteen models projects, as a section through the camera centre and as the ray field it gives on the sphere.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Per-point error on the eight camera models. Same cells and same viewpoints as Fig. 6, with colour giving each point’s distance to the ground truth as a fraction of the scene radius. The colour scale is shared across all cells.
figures.headline: Per-point error on the eight training cameras, on one shared scale, shows where each method's points stray from ground truth.
citing_sentences: Fig. 9 redraws the same cells with every point coloured by its distance to the ground truth, normalised by the scene radius, which is the quantity Acc averages.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: One checkpoint with and without the ray map. Ray map is the true ray field and Fallback is the equirectangular one the backbone assumes when none is supplied. Colour is distance to the ground truth as a fraction of the scene radius, on the scale of Fig. 9. Every camera degrades when the ray map is withdrawn except the equirectangular one in the last row, where the fallback coincides with the true field and nothing changes.
figures.headline: Withdrawing the ray map degrades every camera except equirectangular, where the fallback equals the true field and nothing changes.
citing_sentences: Fig. 10 shows two of them on the same frames.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: The eight central camera models. The same $360^{\circ}$ panorama imaged through each lens, so every difference in distortion and in coverage comes from the camera model alone. Under each panel: field of view, then the fraction of the sphere that lens observes. Overlaid graticule: equator in red, prime meridian in teal, $45^{\circ}$ meridians and $30^{\circ}$ parallels in white, and the region outside the image circle in light grey.
figures.headline: One 360° panorama imaged through the eight central cameras, so distortion and coverage differ only by lens model.
citing_sentences: Fig. 11 images one panorama through each of the eight camera models, with a graticule drawn on the sphere before projection so the distortion each model applies is visible as a deformation of the grid.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: From one panorama to a native camera frame. Top: the source panorama with the footprints of a $90^{\circ}$ pinhole and a $200^{\circ}$ fisheye marked. Middle: the ray map with direction shown as colour, the validity mask, and the resampled image. Bottom: the same panorama through all eight models. A fresh camera is drawn per view during training.
figures.headline: One panorama is resampled through each camera's ray map into a native frame, producing the training views for every model.
citing_sentences: Fig. 12 shows how one such frame is produced.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Acc against field of view, each method normalised by its own $90^{\circ}$ value and averaged over the three datasets. The left panel shows all seven general-purpose methods and the right one Any3R and the three that degrade least, on a magnified scale. Below one means the wider lens is the easier one for that method.
figures.headline: Normalised by each method's own 90° Acc, the curves show how Acc changes with field of view, with Any3R on a magnified scale.
citing_sentences: Fig. 13 plots the five field-of-view bands of Tab. 15 with each method divided by its own Acc at $90^{\circ}$ and averaged over the three datasets of the paired pool, so the curves start together and only the slope is compared.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Real pinhole imagery on three DL3DV scenes with three views each. Every method fuses its own per-view points with its own predicted poses, one similarity transform fitted on the tracks of the released structure-from-motion reconstruction places each cloud, and each row is rendered from one viewpoint. Sky pixels are found once per input image and removed from every method, and each cloud drops its own farthest $10\%$ of points from its own cameras.
figures.headline: On three real pinhole DL3DV scenes, each method's own predicted poses place its points, rendered from one viewpoint per row.
citing_sentences: Fig. 14 shows reconstructions on the same capture set.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: One camera per row, one crop per column, on Matterport3D. The inset in each cell is the input that produced it, and the pair of numbers is its Acc and the field of view left after cropping. The viewpoint is shared along a row, so a row shows the field of view narrowing and the reconstruction shrinking together.
figures.headline: On Matterport3D, narrowing the field of view by cropping shrinks each camera's reconstruction along with it.
citing_sentences: Fig. 15 shows one scene, camera by camera and crop by crop.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Accuracy against field of view with the camera held fixed. Each input is centre-cropped to $1.00$, $0.75$, $0.50$, $0.35$ and $0.20$ of its width and resized back, so only the field of view changes. Reading a curve right to left is reading what a narrower lens costs.
figures.headline: With the camera held fixed, centre-cropping and resizing inputs isolates how accuracy changes with field of view alone.
citing_sentences: Fig. 16 traces the other half of the same question, with the camera held fixed and the crop varied.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Convergence of an earlier full run. Forty epochs from the original initialisation on eight A100s, evaluated under the paper protocol at $518{\times}1036$ on equirectangular input. Dashed lines give the released panoramic baseline on the same protocol; the shaded band is the warm-up.
figures.headline: An earlier full run's per-epoch pose accuracy and depth error converge over forty epochs, shown against the panoramic baseline.
citing_sentences: The released model is trained for $40$ epochs from the original initialisation rather than from a warm start and is evaluated only at its selected checkpoint, so Fig. 17 shows the per-epoch pose accuracy and depth error of an earlier full run from the same initialisation, trained on eight A100s, against the released panoramic baseline on the same protocol.

abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/

sections.body: The introduction states the problem and the contributions. Geometry models read every frame as a pinhole image. Earlier adaptations each support a fixed list of camera models, and MapAnything and OmniVGGT take pinhole intrinsics, which cannot describe a field of view of 180° or more. Any3R conditions the positional encoding and the training loss on each pixel's ray direction, so one set of weights serves any central camera. On three datasets with thirteen camera models, with each method using its own predicted poses, Any3R is most accurate on wide-angle and panoramic lenses and on par with the strongest pinhole baseline at 90°. Its margin over pinhole models is smallest at 90°.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Pinhole-only geometry models cannot mix wide and panoramic cameras, and Any3R addresses this with per-pixel ray directions.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into two lines. Feed-forward geometry models assume pinhole input, and MapAnything and OmniVGGT accept optional intrinsics, which is the closest prior setting. A second line handles wide lenses by changing the operator, through spherical convolutions, resampled charts or monocular panoramic depth, so each method fits one projection. The closest work, G-ray, parameterises the rotary phase by camera-local ray angles but evaluates pinhole and fisheye crops, while Any3R mixes eight central camera models from 90° to 360°. The section also states a constraint: a reused pretrained rotary encoding must reproduce the ray angle exactly where they agree, or its prior is lost.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior feed-forward models assume pinhole input, and camera-specific methods each fix one projection, so a change of lens means a change of model.

sections.body: The camera is reduced to its ray field, a unit ray for each pixel with a validity mask, so the network sees no lens type or distortion coefficient. The dense head predicts one distance per pixel along that ray. Training uses half native panoramas and half views resampled from panoramas, with a camera drawn per view from eight central models, field of view in [30°, 360°], and view count from 2 to 8. Angular coordinates replace the pixel index in the rotary positional encoding, and the absolute position term follows the ray angle of each patch. The point loss is weighted by the solid angle each pixel covers, computed from the partial derivatives of the ray field and normalised over valid pixels, so the loss magnitude and learning-rate schedule are unchanged.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Any3R feeds each view's ray field into the rotary encoding and a solid-angle weight into the point loss, so no lens parameters are needed.

sections.body: Any3R is trained for 40 epochs on 32 GH200 GPUs over about 27 hours, on Matterport3D, Stanford2D3DS, Structured3D, PanoCity and DL3DV, with test scenes held out. Evaluation uses 24 scenes per dataset and 3 views per scene, rendered through 13 camera models, eight trained and five held out. Every method fuses its views with its own predicted poses. Acc is the mean distance from a reconstructed point to its nearest ground-truth point, and pose AUC is taken up to 15° and 30°. Among the methods in Table 1, Any3R has the best indoor and outdoor Acc in every training camera cell. Limitation: per-view evaluation raises the mean log10 depth error on Matterport3D from 0.033 to 0.045, which the authors accept for the larger pose gain.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On indoor scenes, Any3R has the lowest Acc on all eight training cameras, from 0.052 m to 0.091 m.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the approach: a backbone conditioned on ray fields through angular coordinates and solid-angle weighting, which handles arbitrary central cameras without calibration search, undistortion or per-lens retraining. It reports the highest reconstruction accuracy with predicted poses across thirteen central camera models and three datasets. It also states that the approach enables scalable reconstruction from smartphone, fisheye surveillance and panoramic imagery. Those applications are not evaluated in the section, and the section adds no new experiment.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: One feed-forward model reconstructs any central camera mix, evaluated on thirteen camera models across three datasets.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the protocol: 24 scenes per dataset with three views each, a pre-registered view rule, and a similarity fit with ICP at 0.1 m indoors and 1.0 m on PanoCity. It covers the five held-out cameras, the zero-shot fisheye samples on ScanNet++ and FIORD, and a pre-registered sign test at p<0.05. Appendix B gives per-dataset accuracy tables, medians, averages over narrow and wide cameras, and a test feeding three cameras into one forward pass. Appendix L compares three rotary-frequency configurations. The released split matches the field-of-view arm on pose, but the constant-angle arm has the lowest median geometry error at 180° and 200°, and the split is 14.0% and 15.9% worse at those fields of view.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists evaluation protocol, per-dataset and per-camera tables, zero-shot fisheye setup, and the rotary-frequency split ablation.
